newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Giscard calls for sharp franc depreciation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Giscard calls for sharp franc depreciation.

text.p: Former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing called on Wednesday for a sharp depreciation in the franc, adding to a increasing chorus of voices looking to use exchange rate policy to breathe life into the economy.

Giscard said in an article in the weekly magazine l'Express France should declare as soon as possible a target for the exchange rate significantly lower than it is now. This target would apply when the franc is locked irrevocably into European monetary union in 1999.

Financial markets would then push the franc down towards this target, lifting the burden on the economy of an overvalued exchange rate against the dollar, itself the result of a "stubborn" insistence on maintaining a link to the mark.

While the pro-European Giscard gave no hint that his argument enjoyed any government support, it found a partial echo in comments by other politicians that suggest France is looking more and more at using exchange rate adjustments as a part of economic policy.
In a radio interview on Tuesday a parliamentarian and member of President Jacques Chirac's RPR party said the strong franc policy followed over the last decade could not go unchanged.

"The policy of the strong franc cannot continue in the manner it is right now," Pierre Mazeaud, head of the National Assembly's legal committee, said on Radio Shalom. "We must also let the franc float a little. What is most important in the short term is a recovery of consumption."
The deeply unpopular government desperately needs an injection of new life into the economy to bring down unemployment from its record 12.6 percent.
But until now, it has looked to exchange rate policy to act as a panacea after monetary union rather than before.
Chirac said in Tokyo on Tuesday Europe needed a powerful currency "to resist the aberrant fluctuations in the dollar".

French officials have often said the dollar is undervalued while the opposition Socialist party has said the dollar should be at parity with the euro -- implying a significant revaluation in the U.S. currency.The afternoon daily Le Monde said on Monday that in private some government ministers shared that view.

Giscard's article, however, was one of the first in years by a high-ranking politician to tackle publicly the taboo question of the franc-mark link -- long seen as the linchpin for monetary union between Europe's two biggest economies.

In it he argued France should announce before the end of the year plans to fix the franc at a rate of seven per euro -- corresponding to a more appropriate level of 5.49 francs per dollar, compared with 5.08 francs currently.
This would correspond to a level of 3.65 francs per mark, against 3.38 today -- still within the 15 percent fluctuation bands permitted under the European Exchange Rate Mechanism.

Giscard said he had always believed the most important decision ahead of monetary union was to decide the rate at which the franc would be fixed, since from 1999, Paris would never again have the option to adjust exchange rates to boost growth.
The franc's current overvaluation against the dollar was a major factor behind France's weak growth and "intolerable" levels of unemployment, he said.

That overvaluation he blamed on a "stubborn" determination to keep the franc level-pegging with the mark, despite a sharp rise in the German currency due to the high German interest rates imposed after unification at the start of the decade.

The franc should be returned to the rate at the start of the 1990s of 5.50 francs per dollar. "If the government let its intention be known to fix a parity of seven francs for one euro, corresponding to 5.50 francs per dollar, we would have within six to nine months a significant acceleration in growth."

The franc dipped to 3.3845 per mark from 3.3797 per mark on Tuesday on the comments by Giscard and Mazeaud, which coincided with an article in Le Monde highlighting that the mandate for two members of the independent Bank of France's monetary policy council (CPM) expires at the end of the year.
Le Monde noted this would be a test of the government's commitment to the strong franc.
The mandates for Bruno de Maulde and Jean Boissonat -- two of the six lay members on the CPM -- expires on January 6, 1994, three years after the council was set up.
Both can have their term of office renewed, or they can be replaced by nominees from the presidents of the upper and lower houses of parliament and the Economic and Social Council.
The Bank of France and government officials have so far declined comment on the CPM nominations.
